paragraphs: This paper studies how to minimize functions more quickly using descent algorithms. Its scope includes both convex and nonconvex objectives, and it introduces a first-order method called rescaled gradient descent, or RGD. The central result is conditional: RGD converges faster than ordinary gradient descent when the objective satisfies a property the authors call strong smoothness.

Strong smoothness generalizes the usual smoothness assumption on an objective function. It supplies the additional structure behind the faster convergence result, so the paper does not claim that rescaling improves optimization for every function. The authors also provide examples of machine-learning loss functions with this property, connecting the theoretical condition to concrete optimization problems.

For convex objectives, the paper develops two frameworks for accelerating descent methods, following the approaches of Nesterov and of Monteiro and Svaiter. Both can accelerate RGD under the same strong smoothness assumption. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings. Together, these results identify a function property that can justify faster first-order optimization and show how it interacts with two acceleration strategies.
neurips-2019-accelerating-rescaled-gradi.tldr: Rescaled gradient descent achieves faster convergence under strong smoothness, with further acceleration available for convex objectives.

paragraphs: This paper examines generative adversarial networks through an energy-based modeling interpretation to extract useful representations from them. In this formulation, the discriminator describes an unnormalized probability density through a negative energy function. That interpretation gives its output a role in characterizing the data, supporting feature extraction even where the traditional convergence picture suggests a constant discriminator.

The authors derive Fisher Scores and Fisher Information from the energy-based formulation to evaluate both the generator and discriminator. These quantities lead to normalized Fisher Vectors that can serve as features. Their computational argument relies on an explicit assumption: generated examples provide an estimate of the learned density. Under that assumption, the relevant Fisher quantities are easy to compute.

The framework also yields distances between individual examples and between sets of examples. Experiments find that the resulting GAN-based Fisher Vectors are competitive as unsupervised features for classification and perceptual similarity. The contribution is therefore both an interpretation of what a discriminator represents and a practical way to turn that representation into features and comparison measures.
neurips-2019-adversarial-fisher-vectors-.tldr: An energy-based interpretation of GANs yields Fisher Vector features with competitive performance on classification and perceptual similarity tasks.

paragraphs: Eigendecomposition supplies eigenvectors that deep networks can use to transform their features, but passing learning signals backward through this operation can be numerically unstable. The paper identifies this problem in both direct eigendecomposition and Power Iteration approximations, particularly for large matrices. This makes the backward computation a practical obstacle to using the operation inside trainable networks.

A workaround is to divide data into small groups before applying eigendecomposition. The authors argue that these arbitrary divisions lack a theoretical basis and prevent the operation from being used to its full extent. They introduce a differentiable, numerically stable approach that can use eigenvectors from large matrices without requiring such a split.

The paper demonstrates improved robustness over standard eigendecomposition and Power Iteration in two settings. One is ZCA whitening, used as an alternative to batch normalization. The other is PCA denoising, introduced here as a normalization strategy intended to further remove noise from network features. These results support the method's usefulness for incorporating eigenvector-based feature processing into deep-network training.
neurips-2019-backpropagation-friendly-ei.tldr: A stable differentiable approach lets deep networks use eigenvectors from large matrices without splitting the data into small groups.

paragraphs: Extreme classification involves choosing among very large collections of labels. The paper investigates why neural classifiers based on embeddings had lagged behind sparse linear and tree-based approaches in accuracy. Earlier explanations often blamed the low dimensionality of the embeddings. The authors challenge that explanation with a theoretical result showing that low-dimensional embeddings do not impose the proposed limitation.

Their experiments instead point to overfitting as the cause of poor performance. This shifts the focus toward how the models learn from their training data. The authors investigate data augmentation and regularization, introducing GLaS, a regularizer that generalizes graph Laplacian and spread-out regularization. Empirically, it addresses drawbacks that arise when either of those regularizers is used alone in extreme classification.

With these techniques, the models match or improve the state of the art on most of the widely tested public datasets considered, including datasets with hundreds of thousands of labels. The findings support a different diagnosis of the performance gap: improving generalization can make embedding-based approaches competitive without treating low-dimensional representations as an inherent barrier.
neurips-2019-breaking-the-glass-ceiling-.tldr: The paper identifies overfitting as an empirical obstacle for extreme classification and introduces regularization that makes embedding-based models competitive.

paragraphs: Correlation clustering groups items using pairwise labels that say whether two items are similar or dissimilar. A clustering makes a disagreement when it separates a similar pair or joins a dissimilar pair. The usual objective counts all disagreements together. This paper instead studies objectives that account for how those disagreements are distributed across individual items or clusters.

For each item, the authors count the disagreements involving it, forming a vector of local error counts. They study minimizing its lq norm for q at least one, providing a family of ways to summarize these local errors. The paper gives the first known algorithm for this objective on arbitrary graphs and an improved algorithm for complete graphs, where every pair has an edge.

The authors also address a cluster-level objective: minimizing the largest number of disagreements associated with any cluster. They obtain an improved approximation factor of 2 plus epsilon. These contributions broaden clustering beyond a single total error count, supplying algorithms for objectives that explicitly consider where disagreements fall within the resulting partition.
neurips-2019-correlation-clustering-with.tldr: New correlation-clustering algorithms optimize disagreement counts at the item and cluster levels rather than only their overall total.

paragraphs: Generating dance from music requires coordinating several kinds of information at once. Movements need to relate to musical style and beat, while also forming a plausible dance sequence. There is no single correct continuation of a pose: several next movements can be equally suitable. The paper treats this diversity as part of the generation problem.

The proposed framework learns through two connected phases. In the analysis phase, it breaks dances into basic movement units, allowing the model to learn how those movements work. In the synthesis phase, it learns to combine multiple units into a complete dance according to the input music, with seamless connections between the component movements.

This division separates learning movement elements from learning how to arrange them musically. Qualitative and quantitative experiments indicate that the method can generate dances that are realistic, varied, consistent in style, and aligned with the beat. The stated findings address both sides of the task: producing credible motion and making that motion correspond to the music.
neurips-2019-dancing-to-music-8bb220d6b5.tldr: A framework that learns basic dance movements and then combines them generates diverse dances aligned with musical style and beat.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate differences between two graphical models when each measured variable is a function. An EEG signal, for example, is naturally a curve over time rather than a single number. Such data create two sources of complexity: a sample can contain many functions, and each function is itself an infinite-dimensional object.

The authors consider two undirected graphical models with shared structure and develop a method that estimates their difference directly. This avoids separately estimating both full graphs before comparing them. The approach concentrates the estimation task on the change between the models, which is the quantity the paper seeks to recover.

The theoretical analysis establishes consistency in certain high-dimensional settings, giving a qualified guarantee for the proposed estimator. Simulations examine its behavior with finite samples. An application to EEG data investigates differences in functional brain connectivity between people with alcoholism and control subjects. Together, these parts connect a targeted estimation method with both mathematical guarantees and an application involving time-varying measurements.
neurips-2019-direct-estimation-of-differ.tldr: The method directly estimates differences between graphs of functional measurements, with consistency in certain high-dimensional settings and an EEG application.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how symbolic knowledge can help deep models. Its inputs include propositional formulas and assignments, which carry logical meaning as well as structure. The proposed graph embedding network maps these objects into a learned geometric representation using an augmented graph convolutional network, making symbolic information available in a form usable by neural models.

Preserving meaning during that mapping is a central concern. The method distinguishes different types of nodes and uses semantic regularization to incorporate structural constraints into the embeddings. These components aim to make the learned representations faithful to the symbolic objects, so their usefulness depends on more than simply turning a graph into a vector.

Experiments report improvements on entailment checking and visual relation prediction. The authors also observe a connection between how tractable a propositional theory's representation is and how easily it can be embedded. They present further study of that connection as a possible route to understanding the relationship between knowledge compilation and vector representation learning, rather than as an already established general result.
neurips-2019-embedding-symbolic-knowledg.tldr: A graph embedding network incorporates logical structure into neural representations and improves entailment checking and visual relation prediction.

paragraphs: Mixed packing and covering linear programs are a class of optimization problems used in combinatorial optimization and operations research. This paper gives an algorithm that finds a 1 plus epsilon approximate solution in O(Nw/epsilon) time. Here N counts nonzero entries in the constraint matrix, and w is the largest number of nonzero entries in any constraint.

The algorithm uses area convexity to remove a square-root dependence on problem dimension that appears in the stated comparison with Nesterov's smoothing algorithm. Its dependence on precision is also better than that of the cited width-independent method, whose runtime scales as O(N/epsilon squared). This comparison involves a tradeoff because the new method still depends on w.

Small-width problems are therefore particularly relevant: the authors explain that their method can obtain higher precision in such cases compared with width-independent algorithms. As a special case, they derive a 1 plus epsilon approximation for the densest subgraph problem in O(md/epsilon) time, where m counts edges and d is the maximum degree.
neurips-2019-faster-width-dependent-algo.tldr: An area-convexity algorithm improves precision dependence for mixed packing-covering linear programs, with particular benefits when constraints have small width.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a viewed image from fMRI requires learning a relationship between images and brain recordings. Paired examples are scarce, and collecting enough to cover the variety of natural images is prohibitive. This paper expands the training material available to a reconstruction network by also using images without recordings and recordings without their corresponding images.

The model contains two networks with opposite directions. An encoder maps images to fMRI, while a decoder maps fMRI to images. Joining them in either order creates a round trip: image to recording and back, or recording to image and back. These compositions provide self-supervision from each kind of unpaired data.

A particularly relevant consequence is that the reconstruction model can train on the test fMRI inputs without access to their associated images. This lets it adapt to new recordings whose statistics differ from those of the small paired training set. The contribution is a way to use otherwise unpaired observations for training and adaptation in a setting where complete image-recording pairs are difficult to obtain.
neurips-2019-from-voxels-to-pixels-and-b.tldr: Paired image-to-fMRI and fMRI-to-image networks enable self-supervised training on unpaired data, including adaptation to unlabeled test recordings.

paragraphs: This paper uses natural language as an intermediate representation for deciding how an agent should act. The agent first generates an instruction that expresses a plan, and a separate model executes it through lower-level actions. Language therefore becomes part of the decision process, connecting the choice of a complex action with the steps needed to carry it out.

The authors introduce a real-time strategy environment that requires coordinating many units over long periods. They collect 76 thousand instruction-and-execution pairs from human play and use them to train instructor and executor models. This provides examples of both what a player intends to do and how that intention is expressed through actions.

Experiments show that models using language as a latent variable significantly outperform models that directly imitate human actions. The paper also finds that language's compositional structure is crucial to its effectiveness as an action representation. The results support organizing complex behavior around instructions whose parts can combine meaningfully, with separate models responsible for planning and execution.
neurips-2019-hierarchical-decision-makin.tldr: Agents that generate and execute natural-language plans outperform direct action imitation in a strategy environment requiring long-term coordination.

paragraphs: This paper studies how the prior distribution in a variational autoencoder shapes its learned latent representation. The authors target over-regularization associated with a standard normal prior. They propose learning a hierarchical prior so that the representation is not governed solely by that fixed distribution, with the aim of retaining informative structure about the data.

The learning objective is formulated as a constrained optimization problem. Specifically, the work extends the Taming VAEs framework to a two-level hierarchical model. The constraints are intended to encourage informative latent representations, while the learned prior participates in shaping how the data are organized within that representation.

The authors also introduce a graph-based method for interpolation. Using it, they show correspondence between the topology of the learned latent representation and that of the data manifold. Several examples illustrate the prior learning desirable properties, including smoothness and simple explanatory factors. These examples connect the proposed training formulation to the organization of the resulting latent space, beyond simply specifying a more elaborate prior.
neurips-2019-learning-hierarchical-prior.tldr: Learning a hierarchical VAE prior helps address over-regularization and produces latent representations with useful structure in the presented examples.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential control of linear dynamical systems when the cost of decisions can change adversarially over time. It assumes that the system's transition dynamics are known and that the cost functions are strongly convex. The setting encompasses influential control frameworks, including the Kalman filter and the linear quadratic regulator.

The performance question concerns regret: how the accumulated cost of online decisions compares with the relevant benchmark over a horizon of T steps. Previously available methods in this setting achieved regret growing as the square root of T. The authors show that the achievable dependence can be substantially smaller, growing only polylogarithmically with T.

Two efficient iterative methods attain the stated bound: online gradient descent and online natural gradient. The result matters because it sharpens what is achievable even when costs change adversarially, rather than following a predictable pattern. Its scope remains tied to the specified assumptions of known linear dynamics and strongly convex costs; within that setting, it establishes a much slower growth of regret with time.
neurips-2019-logarithmic-regret-for-onli.tldr: With known linear dynamics and strongly convex adversarial costs, efficient online control methods achieve polylogarithmic regret.

paragraphs: Privacy guarantees can fail because of errors in either a mechanism's design or its implementation. This paper studies a data-driven way to assess approximate differential privacy using black-box access to a mechanism on neighboring databases. It treats the task as estimating a property from samples and asks how estimation accuracy depends on the number of observations.

The proposed estimator uses polynomial approximation with a carefully selected degree. That choice balances bias and variance, two competing sources of estimation error. The resulting method makes more effective use of the available samples than a straightforward plug-in estimator, which directly substitutes empirical estimates into the quantity being measured.

The authors show that their estimator with n samples achieves the performance of the plug-in approach with n times log(n) samples. They call this effective sample size amplification. A matching fundamental lower bound establishes minimax optimality. The contribution therefore combines a concrete estimator with a characterization of the best possible accuracy-sample tradeoff for the studied privacy-estimation problem.
neurips-2019-minimax-optimal-estimation-.tldr: A minimax-optimal estimator uses polynomial approximation to estimate privacy guarantees more efficiently from black-box samples.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows represent complicated probability distributions by transforming a simple base distribution through an invertible mapping. Coupling and autoregressive flows support exact density evaluation and sampling, but their flexibility depends on the individual transformations they use. Those transformations must be expressive while still allowing the mapping to be reversed efficiently.

The paper introduces a fully differentiable module built from monotonic rational-quadratic splines. These provide a more flexible choice of elementwise transformation while retaining an analytic inverse. The module can be used with both coupling and autoregressive constructions, so the contribution applies to two established ways of building flow models.

The authors demonstrate improvements in density estimation, variational inference, and image generation. These findings connect the choice of transformation inside a flow to its usefulness across several modeling tasks. The approach matters because increased expressiveness comes while preserving analytic invertibility, a property central to the flow construction. It changes a building block of the model while keeping the exact density and sampling capabilities that motivate these architectures.
neurips-2019-neural-spline-flows-26753ac.tldr: Monotonic rational-quadratic splines make normalizing flows more flexible while preserving analytic invertibility.

paragraphs: Black-box optimization repeatedly tests configurations to discover good ones. When several tasks need optimization, there is another decision to make: which task should receive the next test? This paper studies an offline setting where the optimizer can choose that task, for example through a simulator, instead of having it determined by external circumstances.

The authors propose a theoretically grounded Bayesian optimization method that considers both task selection and configuration selection. This matters because tasks can differ in difficulty and importance. Allocating evaluations therefore requires reasoning about where another test will be useful, as well as which configuration looks promising within the chosen task.

The paper also demonstrates a specific risk: actively choosing tasks may do more harm than good when the reward model poorly captures differences in task difficulty. This makes the model's representation of cross-task variation central to the approach. Applications in science and engineering, including tokamak control optimization for nuclear fusion, illustrate how the method can be used when evaluations can be directed across tasks.
neurips-2019-offline-contextual-bayesian.tldr: A Bayesian optimization method chooses both tasks and configurations, while showing how poor modeling of task difficulty can undermine active task selection.

paragraphs: Segmented linear regression trees divide data into regions and assign a linear predictor to each terminal node. This paper proposes a way to learn that partitioning structure. At each node, an adaptive procedure chooses a split using a criterion based on conditional Kendall's tau, measuring rank dependence between the predictors and the residuals of the fitted linear model.

The split criterion connects the remaining pattern in the residuals to the decision to subdivide a region. The theoretical analysis shows that the procedure permits consistent identification and estimation of unknown segments. Repeated splitting first builds a sufficiently large tree, after which cost-complexity pruning selects its size while preserving nested subtrees and consistent estimation of the number of segments.

The authors also use these trees as base predictors for random forests and a proposed weighted random forest method. Simulations and empirical studies evaluate the individual trees and ensembles. On well-studied public datasets, the empirical results show advantageous predictive performance compared with a set of leading tree-based models.
neurips-2019-partitioning-structure-lear.tldr: A residual-dependence split criterion learns segmented linear regression trees, with consistency results and strong empirical performance for trees and ensembles.

paragraphs: Evaluating a new contextual bandit policy from logged data can avoid costly exploration, but standard approaches usually assume that no relevant confounders are unobserved. This paper considers a different setting: confounders remain latent, but proxies for them are available. The authors develop an importance-weighting method without fitting a latent outcome regression model.

A central theoretical finding explains why this setting is difficult. There is no single set of weights that yields unbiased policy evaluation for every outcome model. This differs from the unconfounded case, where density ratios are sufficient. The result identifies a boundary on what a universal weighting solution can accomplish when confounders are hidden.

The proposed method instead chooses weights by minimizing an adversarial objective designed to ensure sufficient balance in the latent confounders regardless of the outcome model. The paper characterizes consistency theoretically and provides tractable algorithms. Empirical results support the approach when confounders are latent. Its contribution combines an impossibility result with a constructive balancing strategy for evaluation using proxy information.
neurips-2019-policy-evaluation-with-late.tldr: Proxy-based adversarial balancing enables policy evaluation with latent confounders despite the absence of universally unbiased importance weights.

paragraphs: Meta-learning uses experience from previous tasks to make learning a new task more efficient. That shared experience can be less helpful when tasks differ substantially or change over time. This paper addresses the difficulty of deciding which learned inductive bias is appropriate when a stream of tasks does not follow one stable distribution.

The authors build on the connection between gradient-based meta-learning and hierarchical Bayesian modeling. They propose a Dirichlet process mixture of hierarchical Bayesian models over a parametric model's parameters, including those of a neural network. This mixture supports task-dependent hyperparameter selection instead of consolidating all learned biases into a single hyperparameter set.

The approach is evaluated on evolving image-based few-shot learning benchmarks. Those experiments show improved handling of latent distribution shifts through task-dependent selection. The result supports using multiple sources of inductive bias when transfer varies across tasks. The paper's central contribution is to connect meta-learning with an online mixture formulation that can accommodate differences in which prior learning is useful.
neurips-2019-reconciling-meta-learning-a.tldr: A Bayesian mixture selects task-dependent inductive biases to better handle changing task distributions in few-shot learning.

paragraphs: The Sobolev Independence Criterion measures dependence between a high-dimensional input and a response while exposing the contribution of individual features. Its value decomposes into feature-importance scores, making it useful for nonlinear feature selection. The goal is to measure a relationship and identify which parts of the input account for it.

The method compares the joint distribution of inputs and responses with the product of their separate distributions using an integral probability metric. Gradient penalties encourage its critic to depend on a sparse set of inputs. In the kernel formulation, auxiliary variables turn the problem into convex optimization and serve as normalized feature-importance scores. A neural formulation uses a homogeneous neural network to improve representation power and interpretability.

Synthetic and real-world experiments validate the criterion for feature selection. The authors also show reliable, interpretable discoveries when combining it with holdout randomization testing and knockoffs to control the false discovery rate. That qualification matters: the stated discovery control accompanies those additional procedures, rather than following from feature-importance scores alone.
neurips-2019-sobolev-independence-criter.tldr: The Sobolev Independence Criterion measures nonlinear dependence through interpretable feature scores and supports feature selection with additional discovery-control procedures.

paragraphs: Bayesian coresets compress a dataset before applying a standard inference algorithm, aiming to reduce computation while controlling posterior approximation error. Earlier construction methods depended on an initial coarse posterior approximation. This paper targets that dependency, which can be difficult to supply and limits how automatically such methods can be applied.

The authors formulate coreset construction as variational inference with a sparsity constraint inside an exponential family. This leads to a greedy optimization procedure and an information-geometric interpretation that connects the new method with previous approaches. The resulting Riemannian coreset algorithm requires no problem-specific inputs beyond the probabilistic model and dataset.

Experiments show that a fixed coarse posterior approximation can fundamentally constrain earlier coreset constructions. The proposed method can instead continue improving its coreset, with reported reductions of orders of magnitude in KL divergence from the exact posterior. These findings link easier setup to better dataset summarization: removing the fixed approximation requirement also removes the particular restriction on refinement observed in the experiments.
neurips-2019-sparse-variational-inferenc.tldr: A sparse variational formulation builds Bayesian coresets automatically without an initial posterior approximation and substantially improves posterior fidelity in experiments.

paragraphs: Many Markov chain Monte Carlo methods generate samples by numerically approximating continuous-time dynamics. This paper connects the local errors of an integration method to the convergence rate of the resulting sampler. Its general analysis concerns smooth Ito diffusions that contract quickly in 2-Wasserstein distance, a measure of discrepancy between probability distributions.

The authors apply this analysis to stochastic Runge-Kutta discretization of overdamped Langevin dynamics. For strongly convex potentials with sufficient higher-order smoothness, they establish convergence in approximately O(d times epsilon to the power minus two-thirds) iterations, with logarithmic factors suppressed. This improves the stated best-known rate for unadjusted, gradient-only sampling based on the overdamped Langevin equation in the strongly log-concave setting.

The analysis also extends to uniformly dissipative diffusions whose potentials may be nonconvex. There, stochastic Runge-Kutta methods improve dependence on the tolerance epsilon compared with Euler-Maruyama discretization. Numerical studies report better stability and lower asymptotic errors. The contribution shows how the numerical integration scheme can improve sampling performance under the specified properties of the underlying dynamics.
neurips-2019-stochastic-runge-kutta-acce.tldr: Stochastic Runge-Kutta discretization improves sampling convergence under stated smoothness and dynamical assumptions, with better stability in numerical studies.

paragraphs: Structured prediction requires choosing outputs with internal organization, such as rankings or collections of labels. This paper provides a framework for constructing loss functions from a geometric description of those outputs. The user selects a convex set containing the output space and supplies a procedure for projecting onto that set; the framework then produces a convex, smooth loss.

The authors prove that adding a projection at the output layer makes the loss smaller. They identify the convex hull of the output space, called the marginal polytope, as the best set for projection. Because that projection can be expensive, the framework also accepts larger convex sets whose projections may be cheaper to compute.

The theoretical guarantee links these losses to a target loss that may be nonconvex: combined with calibrated decoding, they provide a consistent surrogate. Experiments on label ranking, ordinal regression, and multilabel classification confirm accuracy improvements from projections. The framework thus connects available projection algorithms with trainable losses while exposing a choice between the preferred geometry and computational convenience.
neurips-2019-structured-prediction-with-.tldr: Projection procedures generate smooth convex losses for structured prediction, with conditional consistency guarantees and demonstrated accuracy improvements.

paragraphs: Anomaly labels are difficult to collect because unusual events are rare. Transferring knowledge from related domains can help, but existing methods described in the paper require training for each target domain. The proposed approach instead infers a target-domain anomaly detector from its normal examples without retraining, reducing the need for target-specific optimization.

The key representation is a latent domain vector inferred from a set of normal instances. This vector controls the domain-specific behavior of an autoencoder-based anomaly score. Training encourages normal instances to receive low scores and anomalies to score higher, while accounting for uncertainty in the domain vectors. The same framework can also incorporate target normal examples during training when they are available.

Experiments use one synthetic dataset and four real-world datasets. The authors report that their method without retraining outperforms existing approaches that perform target-specific training. These results support learning how normal data characterize a domain so that a suitable detector can be inferred for it, rather than requiring a separate training procedure for every target.
neurips-2019-transfer-anomaly-detection-.tldr: Latent vectors inferred from normal examples let an anomaly detector adapt to target domains without retraining, with strong reported experimental results.

paragraphs: Predicting the next event in an asynchronous sequence requires reasoning from a history in which events need not arrive at regular intervals. The prediction can change as more time passes, even before another event occurs. This paper focuses on representing that evolution together with uncertainty, including times when a confident prediction may not be possible.

The authors introduce two architectures, WGP-LN and FD-Dir. They model time-dependent distributions over probability vectors using logistic-normal and Dirichlet distributions. Recurrent neural networks are combined with Gaussian processes or function decomposition to express how the distribution parameters evolve. This construction lets the model represent uncertainty alongside changing event probabilities.

Experiments evaluate event-class prediction, event-time prediction, and anomaly detection across several datasets, reporting strong performance compared with other approaches. These tasks test different uses of the same temporal uncertainty modeling. The contribution is to treat a prediction as a distribution that evolves with elapsed time, giving the model a way to express both changing expectations and varying confidence about the next event.
neurips-2019-uncertainty-on-asynchronous.tldr: Two architectures model how next-event probabilities and uncertainty evolve over time, supporting event prediction and anomaly detection.
